result:
The first thing my father fixed after he retired was the kitchen clock. It had been seven minutes fast since I was nine. He took it down, set it by the radio, and hung it back up.

“What was wrong with it?” I asked.

“Nothing,” he said. “I used to need the seven minutes.”

He’d built them into the morning when my sister and I were little. Seven minutes to find a shoe, turn a permission slip over and discover the other place he had to sign, or stand at the end of the driveway while one of us ran back to the house to pee. We knew the clock was fast. He knew we knew. We still believed it when we were late.

That afternoon I went with him to the hardware store. He needed a washer for the outside tap. The man at the counter asked what size, and my father pulled the old one from his shirt pocket, wrapped in a square of paper towel.

On the way home he took the road past my old school. There was a little girl at the crossing with one arm out of her coat. Her father held her backpack while she tried to get the sleeve right side out. The crossing guard had already stepped into the road, so we waited.

My father drummed his fingers once on the steering wheel. Then he turned off the radio so we could hear what the girl was saying.

“I can do it,” she said. “Hold my other stuff.”
